title: Gas analysis system for studying sand mold’s atmosphere during steel casting
author: Wielgosz, Vaucheret, et al.
materials: The presented system has been developed at ENSAM Cluny (LaBoMaP) in collaboration with the industrial partner – Safe Metal. It should be noted that as far the laboratory was not equipped with any scientific instrument enabling quantitative analysis of the gas composition. The idea behind the development was to use off-the-shelf gas sensors to create a gas analyzer, appropriate to foundry, to enable the study of the gas composition on site. Following design assumptions about the system were made at the beginning of the project:•Mobility – the system needs to be moved around easily so that it does not stay in the foundry laboratory permanently,•Capability to quantify gases which are known to be the main constituents of the mold’s atmosphere (H2, CO, CO2, CH4 and O2),•Capacity to acquire analog signal from external instruments such as pressure transducers and thermocouples,•Capacity of continuous online gas measurement during casting.•System must be adapted to the sand-casting process by proper conditioning of the sample prior to the analysis.•Ability to control and regulate flowrate during gas extraction.

H2 sensor, CH4 sensor, CO sensors (1 & 2) as well as CO2 sensors (1 & 2) feature digital outputs and use Modbus RTU protocol for communication. Furthermore, sensors are equipped with analogue outputs 0–10 V (H2 sensor) or 4–20 mA (CO2 sensor 1, CO sensor 1, CH4 sensor, O2 sensor) related linearly to the measured gas concentration. Flowrate sensor D6F-01A1–110 has an analogue output 0–5 V which is related to the reading by means of a quadratic function. NI-9205 card, used with Compact DAQ, featuring 32 analogue input channels (voltage) is used to register analogue signals. Voltage outputs are connected directly to the DAC card whereas the output current is measured indirectly by passing the current through a high precision 500 Ohm resistor (±0.01 %) and measuring the voltage across its terminals. As far as CO sensor 2 and CO2 sensor 2 are concerned the sensor readings are acquired from the numerical signal using a USB adapter and dedicated software provided by the manufacturers.

steps.title: Mount system on mobile trolley
steps.instruction: Place the entire gas‑analysis assembly on a SERVI‑3P2T tray‑tool trolley (SAM) so the upper tier can be used as the operator work surface, the middle tier holds sensors, pumps and filters (elements 3, 4, 6‑16) and the lower tier contains the airtight box (17‑19) together with the power‑supply and data‑acquisition boxes.

steps.title: Insert stainless‑steel sampling tube
steps.instruction: Insert the stainless‑steel (SS) tube (element 2) into the sand mould at the desired sampling location; this tube will convey the gas to the diaphragm pump (element 9).

steps.title: Start gas extraction
steps.instruction: Activate the diaphragm pump (9) and switch the 3/2 solenoid valve (3) to the sampling position so that gas is drawn from the mould through the SS tube.

steps.title: Condition the sampled gas
steps.instruction: Pass the drawn gas sequentially through the conditioning train:

substeps.instruction: 2 µm particle filter (4) to remove sand fines.
Gas cooler (5) – a JCM‑300 Peltier cooler – to lower the gas temperature below 0 °C; condensate is removed via a capillary at the bottom of the U‑tube.
Optional silica‑gel tube placed downstream of the cooler to increase drying performance.
Liquid‑stop filter (7) that clogs if liquid condensation reaches it, providing a safety stop.

steps.title: Control and monitor flowrate
steps.instruction: Adjust the Key Instruments FR2000 flowmeter (8), which is calibrated on air, to set the desired gas flow; the flow sensor (19) in the airtight box (18) is also calibrated on air and provides an indirect flow‑rate measurement as the Tedlar bag (17) fills.

steps.title: Measure gas concentrations with sensors
steps.instruction: Route the conditioned gas past the single‑gas sensors (10‑16) that measure H₂, CO, CO₂, CH₄ and O₂ according to the specifications in Table 1:

substeps.instruction: H₂ sensor (thermal conductivity) – 0‑100 vol % range, t₉₀ < 5 s.
CO₂ sensor 1 (NDIR) – 0‑50 vol % range, t₉₀ < 3 s.
CH₄ sensor (NDIR) – 0‑15 vol % range, t₉₀ < 3 s.
CO sensor 1 (NDIR) – 0‑100 vol % range, t₉₀ < 3 s.
O₂ sensor (paramagnetic) – 0‑25 vol % range, t₉₀ < 3 s, constant flow 150 ml s⁻¹ through its bypass.
CO sensor 2 (NDIR) – 0‑100 vol % range, t₉₀ < 14 s.
CO₂ sensor 2 (NDIR) – 0‑100 vol % range, t₉₀ < 30 s.

steps.title: Collect gas in Tedlar bag
steps.instruction: Direct the measured gas into a Tedlar bag (17) that sits inside the airtight box (18); as the bag fills, air is expelled through the outlet and measured by flow sensor (19).

steps.title: Acquire data on PC
steps.instruction: Connect the NI data‑acquisition cart (20) to the PC (21) via USB; use DASYLab software to record analogue (0‑10 V or 4‑20 mA converted via 500 Ω resistor) and digital (Modbus RTU) outputs from all sensors, as well as thermocouple inputs from the two NI‑9212 cards.

steps.title: Calibrate oxygen sensor
steps.instruction: Perform zero‑span calibration of the O₂ sensor:

substeps.instruction: Zero: supply an oxygen‑free gas and adjust the zero potentiometer until the reading is 0 % O₂.
Span: supply ambient air (≈21 % O₂) and adjust the span potentiometer until the reading matches 21 % O₂.

steps.title: Verify other sensors are factory‑calibrated
steps.instruction: Confirm that all sensors except the O₂ sensor are factory‑calibrated; no further adjustment is required before measurements.

steps.title: Calculate repeatability statistics
steps.instruction: For each gas, compute the standard deviation σ using σ = √[ Σ(x − u)² / (n − 1) ], where x are the average concentrations of individual peaks, u is the mean of all peaks, and n is the number of peaks.

steps.title: Assess signal stability visually
steps.instruction: Examine the derivative of each sensor’s reading; consider the signal stable when the maximum derivative is at least twice the maximum derivative observed for the noise while reading air.

steps.title: Collect mould gas for µGC comparison
steps.instruction: Prepare three green‑sand mould samples (sand humidity = 5.6 %) using reclaimed sand, bentonite and water; pour low‑carbon steel at 1630 °C; draw gas for 10 min with an Artshu MPA2002T2 pump; dry the gas through a silica‑gel tube before filling Tedlar bags; analyse the bags on the same day with a Micro‑GC 3000 (SRA Instruments) at LMI, University of Lyon.

steps.title: Use µGC calibration gases
steps.instruction: Employ the following balance‑nitrogen calibration gases for quantitative µGC analysis:

substeps.instruction: Bottle 1: H₂ = 1995 ± 40 ppm (2.005 mol %).
Bottle 2: CO₂ = 59 ± 0.004 mol %.
Bottle 4: CH₄ = 535 ± 11 ppm.
O₂ = 20 ± 1 mol %.

steps.title: Repeat µGC measurements and compute errors
steps.instruction: For each of the three samples, repeat the µGC analysis four times; calculate standard deviations (Table 9 values) and compare sensor‑derived concentrations with µGC results to obtain relative errors (Table 10).

substeps.instruction: Sample 1 σ: H₂ = 0.036 vol %, CO₂ = 0.019 vol %, CO = 0.001 vol %, O₂ = 0.039 vol %.
Sample 2 σ: H₂ = 0.074 vol %, CO₂ = 0.026 vol %, CO = 0.001 vol %, O₂ = 0.160 vol %.
Sample 3 σ: H₂ = 0.244 vol %, CO₂ = 0.320 vol %, CO = 0.003 vol %, O₂ = 0.174 vol %.

steps.title: Observe minimum gas‑volume limitation
steps.instruction: Note that CO₂ sensor 2 requires at least 1 L of sampled gas to produce a stable reading; therefore casting geometry must generate sufficient gas volume for continuous sampling.
